analysis.one_liner: Lets workers at larger employers earn one hour of paid sick leave for every 30 hours worked.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to four House committees and died there when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015, with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 15 or more employees to let each worker earn at least one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked. Workers could use that time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a sick child, parent, spouse, or close family-equivalent, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking — including seeking medical care, counseling, relocation, or going to court. It was introduced in December 2014, late in the two-year congressional session, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 15 or more employees — including federal, congressional, and GAO employees — who currently have no paid sick days would earn paid time off for their own illness, a sick family member, or to address domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Because low-wage service workers are least likely to have paid sick leave already, they would benefit most.

how_it_helps.text: Employees would earn at least one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, usable for their own illness or medical care.
The leave could also be used to care for a child, parent, spouse, or a close family-equivalent relation who is sick or needs medical care.
Survivors of domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking could use the time for medical attention, counseling, victim services, relocation, or court proceedings related to the abuse.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay for the accrued leave and cover absent workers' shifts; the cost is passed through to businesses rather than taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to employers with 15 or more employees, so workers at smaller businesses would not be covered, and employers would bear a new payroll benefit cost that opponents typically argue falls hardest on low-wage service firms.

The bill does not cap how much paid sick leave an employee can accrue or use in a year, leaving employers no statutory limit on absence costs — a design point an honest supporter would acknowledge invites amendment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers — paid time off when they or a family member are sick or fleeing violence — is substantial and directly costs employers with 15 or more staff a modest payroll benefit. The bill was introduced too late in the Congress and sent to four committees, and died without a hearing or vote, so its costs were never weighed on the record.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House and referred to four committees, none of which took it up, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2014 and referred to four House committees: Education and the Workforce, Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary.
No further action was recorded — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have had to pay the new sick leave benefit are better off; workers who lack paid sick days are left without the protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided a new mandate

for.name: Rep. Alan Grayson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 11, 2014, in the final weeks of the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the bill's support never took a partisan shape on the record.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, food service, and other low-wage service industries in particular)
industries.note: The bill would require these employers to pay for sick leave they do not currently owe, a cost that falls most heavily on industries with many hourly workers. Workers in those same industries are the ones who most often have no paid sick days.
